division_answers.answer:
### [INT] DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR, ENVIRONMENT, AND RELATED AGENCIES
Bottom line: There is no single clean total for these cleanup/remediation lines because the funding spans separate EPA and DOI accounts and mixed program scopes.

Key buckets:
- Brownfields/CERCLA: CERCLA section 104(k) grants are $98,000,000 [[num:src_int_68c231bc_233c_49a7_9433_ff67261f494c_1]], and CERCLA section 128 grants are $46,250,000 [[num:src_int_5cbf3c87_b52e_4290_b96e_19388ea094b7_1]].
- Superfund cleanup: Hazardous Substance Superfund is $282,749,000 [[num:src_int_d632d786_92bc_4a55_9797_b34bbf18c00e_1]] for CERCLA cleanup activities, and CERCLA sections 104(i) and 126(g) are $77,100,000 [[num:src_int_8aeb2531_7161_4e19_84b4_ceb442f34014_1]].
- Other remediation: Leaking Underground Storage Tank Trust Fund Program is $88,903,000 [[num:src_int_676ecc67_2618_41b8_9ebb_1b1dcf5cd4b1_1]], including $64,583,000 [[num:src_int_676ecc67_2618_41b8_9ebb_1b1dcf5cd4b1_2]] for section 9003(h) cleanup; State and Tribal Assistance Grants for remediation projects are $20,364,000 [[num:src_int_c33296d3_2921_4184_b50f_5116bccc7ca8_1]]; grants for remediation of above ground leaking fuel tanks are $2,000,000 [[num:src_int_43a8dd3d_d24d_47a3_afa5_b1919462588e_1]].
- DOI/CERCLA response and related remediation: Central Hazardous Materials Fund is $9,031,000 [[num:src_int_439ec40a_ff5d_4044_9645_66f8f3d503d4_1]], and the Energy Community Revitalization Program is $4,700,000 [[num:src_int_439ec40a_ff5d_4044_9645_66f8f3d503d4_2]].

Local caveat: Environmental Programs and Management is $3,114,671,000 [[num:src_int_50ecf038_8cf4_4344_8029_44323ef53133_1]], but that is a broader EPA account that only includes administrative costs of the brownfields program, so it should not be treated as cleanup-only funding.

final_answer:
### [INT] DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR, ENVIRONMENT, AND RELATED AGENCIES
Bottom line: There is no single clean total for these cleanup/remediation lines because the funding spans separate EPA and DOI accounts and mixed program scopes.

Key buckets:
- Brownfields/CERCLA: CERCLA section 104(k) grants are $98,000,000 [[num:src_int_68c231bc_233c_49a7_9433_ff67261f494c_1]], and CERCLA section 128 grants are $46,250,000 [[num:src_int_5cbf3c87_b52e_4290_b96e_19388ea094b7_1]].
- Superfund cleanup: Hazardous Substance Superfund is $282,749,000 [[num:src_int_d632d786_92bc_4a55_9797_b34bbf18c00e_1]] for CERCLA cleanup activities, and CERCLA sections 104(i) and 126(g) are $77,100,000 [[num:src_int_8aeb2531_7161_4e19_84b4_ceb442f34014_1]].
- Other remediation: Leaking Underground Storage Tank Trust Fund Program is $88,903,000 [[num:src_int_676ecc67_2618_41b8_9ebb_1b1dcf5cd4b1_1]], including $64,583,000 [[num:src_int_676ecc67_2618_41b8_9ebb_1b1dcf5cd4b1_2]] for section 9003(h) cleanup; State and Tribal Assistance Grants for remediation projects are $20,364,000 [[num:src_int_c33296d3_2921_4184_b50f_5116bccc7ca8_1]]; grants for remediation of above ground leaking fuel tanks are $2,000,000 [[num:src_int_43a8dd3d_d24d_47a3_afa5_b1919462588e_1]].
- DOI/CERCLA response and related remediation: Central Hazardous Materials Fund is $9,031,000 [[num:src_int_439ec40a_ff5d_4044_9645_66f8f3d503d4_1]], and the Energy Community Revitalization Program is $4,700,000 [[num:src_int_439ec40a_ff5d_4044_9645_66f8f3d503d4_2]].

Local caveat: Environmental Programs and Management is $3,114,671,000 [[num:src_int_50ecf038_8cf4_4344_8029_44323ef53133_1]], but that is a broader EPA account that only includes administrative costs of the brownfields program, so it should not be treated as cleanup-only funding.

division_answers.answer:
### [CRX] CONTINUING APPROPRIATIONS, EXTENDERS, HOMELAND SECURITY, AND OTHER MATTERS
No dollar total was found in the extracted facts; instead, agencies or accounts covered by the continuing resolution continue temporarily at a rate for operations under the applicable appropriations Acts until a full-year appropriation is enacted or the CR ends.
- Section 101 provides continuing appropriations for covered agencies and accounts when no full-year appropriation is provided, using only the most limited funding action needed to continue projects and activities.
- The authority is temporary: funding continues until an appropriation for the project/activity is enacted, the applicable FY 2026 appropriations Act is enacted without that item, or the CR end date is reached.
- For some costs, amounts may be apportioned up to the rate for operations needed to maintain current operations or avoid furloughs, and payments/reimbursements are limited to amounts provided in advance in appropriations Acts.

### [AG] AGRICULTURE, RURAL DEVELOPMENT, FOOD AND DRUG ADMINISTRATION, AND RELATED AGENCIES
FY2026 in this division treats water infrastructure primarily through USDA Rural Development. The Rural Water and Waste Disposal Program Account receives $445,864,564 [[num:src_ag_4434a248_fea9_4db3_8cc2_78f7b3c7439a_1]] for rural water, wastewater, and waste-disposal needs, including direct loans, grants, and targeted support for distressed communities, tribal communities, and the Department of Hawaiian Home Lands [[num:src_ag_4434a248_fea9_4db3_8cc2_78f7b3c7439a_2]] [[num:src_ag_4434a248_fea9_4db3_8cc2_78f7b3c7439a_3]] [[num:src_ag_4434a248_fea9_4db3_8cc2_78f7b3c7439a_8]] [[num:src_ag_4434a248_fea9_4db3_8cc2_78f7b3c7439a_9]]. It also includes funding for rural utilities, decentralized wastewater systems, and grants under section 306A(i)(2) [[num:src_ag_4434a248_fea9_4db3_8cc2_78f7b3c7439a_4]] [[num:src_ag_4434a248_fea9_4db3_8cc2_78f7b3c7439a_5]] [[num:src_ag_4434a248_fea9_4db3_8cc2_78f7b3c7439a_6]] [[num:src_ag_4434a248_fea9_4db3_8cc2_78f7b3c7439a_7]].

The division also supports water-infrastructure-related technical assistance and source-water protection: $35,000,000 [[num:src_ag_b47d5108_4b53_443f_95f2_5aaf676170de_1]] for technical assistance grants, $23,900,000 [[num:src_ag_b47d5108_4b53_443f_95f2_5aaf676170de_4]] for the circuit rider program, and $7,500,000 [[num:src_ag_dd412d45_228f_441b_a6ec_7436bc3c39cc_1]] for the grassroots source water protection program. The extracted facts provided here do not include EPA or Energy-Water water-infrastructure provisions, so I can only summarize the USDA side from this record.

### [INT] DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR, ENVIRONMENT, AND RELATED AGENCIES

The policy terms favor both core infrastructure and targeted project types: Clean Water SRF grants must dedicate 10 percent to green infrastructure, water or energy efficiency, or other innovative activities, while Drinking Water SRF grants must dedicate 14 percent to additional subsidy and may also be used for similar environmentally innovative projects at state discretion.

I do not have retrieved facts here for USDA or Energy-Water water infrastructure provisions, so this summary is limited to the EPA-related treatment available in the record.

final_answer:
## Answer
FY2026 treats water infrastructure across the three bills in different ways:

- **USDA** funds rural drinking water, wastewater, and waste-disposal infrastructure primarily through the Rural Water and Waste Disposal Program Account at $445,864,564 [[num:src_ag_4434a248_fea9_4db3_8cc2_78f7b3c7439a_1]]. The USDA title also emphasizes targeted support for distressed communities, tribal communities, household decentralized wastewater systems, technical assistance, and source-water protection [[num:src_ag_4434a248_fea9_4db3_8cc2_78f7b3c7439a_3]] [[num:src_ag_4434a248_fea9_4db3_8cc2_78f7b3c7439a_9]] [[num:src_ag_4434a248_fea9_4db3_8cc2_78f7b3c7439a_6]] [[num:src_ag_b47d5108_4b53_443f_95f2_5aaf676170de_1]] [[num:src_ag_dd412d45_228f_441b_a6ec_7436bc3c39cc_1]].

- **EPA** treats water infrastructure as a major capital-financing priority through State and Tribal Assistance Grants totaling $4,409,609,000 [[num:src_int_ff0c97e8_e6fc_4e7e_82bb_c0ede3762000_1]], centered on the Clean Water and Drinking Water State Revolving Funds [[num:src_int_ff0c97e8_e6fc_4e7e_82bb_c0ede3762000_2]] [[num:src_int_ff0c97e8_e6fc_4e7e_82bb_c0ede3762000_3]]. The EPA title also layers in WIFIA assistance, Safe Drinking Water Act and Clean Water Act grants, Alaska drinking water and wastewater support, and policy directives that steer part of the SRF money toward green and innovative projects [[num:src_int_5cbf3c87_b52e_4290_b96e_19388ea094b7_3]] [[num:src_int_68c231bc_233c_49a7_9433_ff67261f494c_1]].

- **Energy-Water** approaches water infrastructure more through project delivery and federal water works: Army Corps civil works, Bureau of Reclamation water programs, regulatory activities, and a small WIFIA credit subsidy for dam-safety lending at $2,200,000 [[num:src_ewd_3b1cadaf_7d55_41a5_aa33_d47df2fc555e_1]]. It also includes a California Bay-Delta restoration appropriation and related guardrails on how water funds may be reprogrammed [[num:src_ewd_26743067_3f79_49b1_bcd1_0a4f76eef148_1]].

In plain English: **USDA focuses on rural systems, EPA focuses on nationwide state revolving fund and grant financing, and Energy-Water focuses on federally carried-out water projects and water-resource infrastructure management.**
